package.title: ITT Notation Fixture: formulae, ions, equations and maths
package.description: A technical fixture for checking scientific typesetting. It carries a formula such as \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\), ions such as \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\), a balanced equation, a fraction, a square root and standard form through every part of a question.
package.subject: Chemistry

author.notes: Written by hand for rendering tests. Import it to see how notation looks before approving real content.

objectives.text: Read and write formulae and ions such as \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\).
Use fractions, roots and standard form, for example \(6.02\times10^{23}\), in calculations.

topics.title: Chemical notation
topics.description: Formulae, ionic charges and balanced equations.

topics.title: Mathematical notation
topics.description: Fractions, powers, roots, standard form and units.

sections.title: Notation in every part of a question
sections.description:
Each question puts notation somewhere different: the question, the choices, the feedback, the key idea and the worked solution. For example, magnesium burns in oxygen:

\[2\mathrm{Mg}+\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow2\mathrm{MgO}\]
sections.purpose: Show formulae, ions, equations and calculations in each field the player typesets.

questions.stem: What is the formula of aluminium oxide?

options.feedback: This would need the charges to be equal and opposite, but an aluminium ion is \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) and an oxide ion is \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\). One of each leaves an overall charge of 1+, so the formula cannot be \(\mathrm{AlO}\).
options.misconception: Pairs one positive ion with one negative ion whatever their charges

options.feedback: The formula of aluminium oxide is \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\), because two aluminium ions, \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\), combine with three oxide ions, \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\), to give an electrically neutral compound: six positive charges balance six negative charges.

The numbers are the right ones but they are attached to the wrong elements. Three \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) ions carry nine positive charges and two \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) ions carry only four negative charges, so \(\mathrm{Al_3O_2}\) would not be neutral.

Two \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) ions carry six positive charges, but a single \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) ion carries only two negative charges. Three oxide ions are needed to balance them, giving \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\).

not_sure.feedback: Start from the ions. Aluminium forms \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) and oxygen forms \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\). Find the smallest numbers of each that make the total positive charge equal the total negative charge.

questions.teaching_note: In an ionic formula the total positive charge equals the total negative charge. The subscripts say how many of each ion are needed: \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) means two \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) for every three \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\).
questions.worked_solution:
Charge from two aluminium ions: \(2\times(+3)=+6\).

Charge from three oxide ions: \(3\times(-2)=-6\).

\[(+6)+(-6)=0\]

The compound is neutral, so the formula is \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\).

questions.stem: Which ion does a sodium atom form?

options.feedback: Sodium is in Group 1 and has one electron in its outer shell. It loses that electron, leaving 11 protons and 10 electrons, so the ion is \(\mathrm{Na^+}\).
A negative ion forms when an atom gains electrons. Sodium is a metal with one outer electron, which it loses rather than gains, so it forms \(\mathrm{Na^+}\), not \(\mathrm{Na^-}\).

A charge of 2+ would mean two electrons had been lost. Sodium has only one electron in its outer shell, so it loses one and forms \(\mathrm{Na^+}\). Magnesium, in Group 2, is the one that forms \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\).
Both the size and the sign are wrong here. An ion such as \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) forms when a non-metal gains two electrons. Sodium is a metal that loses one electron, forming \(\mathrm{Na^+}\).

not_sure.feedback: Use the group number. Sodium is in Group 1, so it has one outer electron. Metals lose their outer electrons, and each electron lost gives one positive charge.

questions.stem:
True or false? This equation is balanced.

\[2\mathrm{Mg}+\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow2\mathrm{MgO}\]

feedback.true: There are two magnesium atoms on each side, and two oxygen atoms on each side: one \(\mathrm{O_2}\) molecule on the left and two \(\mathrm{MgO}\) on the right. The numbers of each kind of atom match, so the equation is balanced.
feedback.false: Count each kind of atom. On the left there are \(2\) magnesium atoms and one \(\mathrm{O_2}\) molecule, which is two oxygen atoms. On the right, \(2\mathrm{MgO}\) contains two magnesium and two oxygen atoms. Both sides match, so the equation is balanced.

not_sure.feedback: An equation is balanced when each kind of atom appears the same number of times on both sides. The large number in front, as in \(2\mathrm{MgO}\), multiplies everything in that formula. The small number, as in \(\mathrm{O_2}\), counts only the atom it follows.

questions.stem:
Calculate the percentage by mass of magnesium in magnesium oxide, \(\mathrm{MgO}\).

Relative atomic masses: \(\mathrm{Mg}=24\), \(\mathrm{O}=16\).

feedback.correct: The relative formula mass of \(\mathrm{MgO}\) is \(24+16=40\), and magnesium contributes 24 of that, so the percentage is \(\frac{24}{40}\times100=60\%\).
feedback.incorrect: Divide the mass of magnesium in the formula by the relative formula mass of the whole compound, then multiply by 100. The formula mass of \(\mathrm{MgO}\) is \(24+16=40\), so the percentage is \(\frac{24}{40}\times100=60\%\).

wrong_answers.feedback: 40 is the percentage of oxygen, \(\frac{16}{40}\times100\). The question asks for magnesium, so the top of the fraction must be 24: \(\frac{24}{40}\times100=60\%\).
150 comes from \(\frac{24}{16}\times100\), which compares magnesium with oxygen. Compare magnesium with the whole compound instead: \(\frac{24}{24+16}\times100=60\%\).
wrong_answers.misconception: Divides by the other element, not the formula mass

not_sure.feedback: Percentage by mass compares one element with the whole compound. Work out the relative formula mass first, \(24+16\), then find what fraction of it is magnesium and multiply by 100.

questions.worked_solution:
Relative formula mass of \(\mathrm{MgO}\):

\[M_r=24+16=40\]

Percentage by mass of magnesium:

\[\frac{24}{40}\times100=60\%\]

questions.stem: A square piece of filter paper has an area of \(49\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). What is the length of one side?

feedback.correct: The area of a square is the side length squared, so the side is the square root of the area: \(\sqrt{49}=7\), and \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\times7\,\mathrm{cm}=49\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).
feedback.incorrect: For a square, \(\text{area}=\text{side}^2\), so the side is the square root of the area. Here \(\sqrt{49}=7\), because \(7^2=49\). The side is \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\).

wrong_answers.feedback: 24.5 is \(49\div2\). Halving undoes doubling, but area comes from squaring, and the operation that undoes squaring is the square root: \(\sqrt{49}=7\).
wrong_answers.misconception: Halves instead of taking the square root

not_sure.feedback: Think about which number multiplied by itself gives 49. That number is the square root of 49, written \(\sqrt{49}\), and it is the length of each side in centimetres.

questions.worked_solution:
The side of a square is the square root of its area:

\[\text{side}=\sqrt{49\,\mathrm{cm^2}}=7\,\mathrm{cm}\]

questions.stem: The Avogadro constant is \(6.02\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\). How many atoms are there in \(2\,\mathrm{mol}\) of carbon?

options.feedback: Two moles contain twice as many atoms as one mole: \(2\times6.02\times10^{23}=12.04\times10^{23}\), which is \(1.204\times10^{24}\) in standard form.
This is \(6.02\times10^{23}\div2\), the number of atoms in half a mole. Two moles contain twice as many atoms as one mole, not half as many: \(2\times6.02\times10^{23}=1.204\times10^{24}\).
options.misconception: Divides by the number of moles

options.feedback: The power of ten has been doubled, which would mean multiplying \(10^{23}\) by itself. Doubling the amount doubles the number in front instead: \(2\times6.02\times10^{23}=1.204\times10^{24}\).
Both the number and the power have been doubled. Only the number in front is multiplied by 2, giving \(12.04\times10^{23}\), which is written \(1.204\times10^{24}\) in standard form.

not_sure.feedback: One mole of atoms is \(6.02\times10^{23}\) atoms. Two moles is twice that. Multiply only the number in front by 2, then check that the answer is in standard form.

questions.stem: Name the ion with the formula \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\).

feedback.correct: \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\) is the sulfate ion: one sulfur atom and four oxygen atoms, with an overall charge of 2−. It is the negative ion in sulfuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).
feedback.incorrect: \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\) is the sulfate ion. The ending "-ate" shows that the ion contains oxygen as well as sulfur. It is the negative ion in sulfuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).

wrong_answers.feedback: A sulfide ion is \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\): sulfur on its own, with no oxygen. When oxygen is part of the ion the name ends in "-ate", so \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\) is sulfate.

not_sure.feedback: Look at which elements are in the ion. A negative ion of one element ends in "-ide", like the sulfide ion \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\). When oxygen is included as well, the name usually ends in "-ate".

sections.title: Independent mastery check
sections.description: Two new questions, one attempt each. The first uses a long equation; the second a calculation with units such as \(\mathrm{mol/dm^3}\).
sections.purpose: Check that long equations and multi-step working stay readable on a narrow screen.

questions.stem:
Aluminium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid:

\[2\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}+3\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\rightarrow\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}+6\mathrm{H_2O}\]

How many hydrogen atoms are there on the left-hand side?

options.feedback: 6 counts only the hydrogen in \(3\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), which is \(3\times2\). The two units of \(\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\) contain hydrogen as well, \(2\times3=6\) more, making 12 in all.
options.misconception: Misses the hydrogen inside the brackets

options.feedback: 9 does not come from multiplying each formula by the number in front of it. \(2\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\) contains \(2\times3=6\) hydrogen atoms and \(3\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) contains \(3\times2=6\), giving 12.
\(2\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\) contains \(2\times3=6\) hydrogen atoms and \(3\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) contains \(3\times2=6\). That is 12, matching the 12 hydrogen atoms in \(6\mathrm{H_2O}\) on the right.

5 adds the small numbers without using the large ones. The number in front multiplies the whole formula: \(2\times3=6\) from \(2\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\) and \(3\times2=6\) from \(3\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), so there are 12.

not_sure.feedback: Take one formula at a time. A subscript after a bracket multiplies everything inside the bracket, and the large number in front multiplies the whole formula. Then add the two results.

questions.stem: \(0.50\,\mathrm{mol}\) of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make \(250\,\mathrm{cm^3}\) of solution. Calculate the concentration in \(\mathrm{mol/dm^3}\).

feedback.correct: \(250\,\mathrm{cm^3}\) is \(0.250\,\mathrm{dm^3}\), and concentration is amount divided by volume: \(\frac{0.50}{0.250}=2.0\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}\).
feedback.incorrect: Convert the volume first: \(250\,\mathrm{cm^3}=0.250\,\mathrm{dm^3}\). Then divide the amount by the volume: \(c=\frac{n}{V}=\frac{0.50}{0.250}=2.0\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}\).

wrong_answers.feedback: 0.002 comes from \(0.50\div250\), which leaves the volume in \(\mathrm{cm^3}\). Divide by 1000 to convert it first: \(250\,\mathrm{cm^3}=0.250\,\mathrm{dm^3}\), and \(\frac{0.50}{0.250}=2.0\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}\).
wrong_answers.misconception: Does not convert cm³ to dm³

wrong_answers.feedback: 0.125 is \(0.50\times0.250\). Concentration is amount divided by volume, not multiplied: \(c=\frac{n}{V}=\frac{0.50}{0.250}=2.0\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}\).

not_sure.feedback: Two steps are needed. There are \(1000\,\mathrm{cm^3}\) in \(1\,\mathrm{dm^3}\), so change the volume into \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) first. Then use \(c=\frac{n}{V}\), the amount in moles divided by the volume.

questions.worked_solution:
Convert the volume:

\[V=\frac{250}{1000}=0.250\,\mathrm{dm^3}\]

Substitute into the equation for concentration:

\[c=\frac{n}{V}=\frac{0.50}{0.250}=2.0\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}\]
